(p-219) Surat an-Nahl is Meccan, except for three verses at its end, and it has one hundred and twenty-eight verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it.﴾ They used to seek to hasten what the Messenger (ﷺ) had threatened them with, namely the Hour's arrival, or Allah's destruction of them as He did on the Day of Badr, out of mockery and denial. They would say: "If what you say is true, then the idols will intercede for us and rescue us from it." So this was revealed. The meaning is that the promised matter is as good as something that has come and is certain, since it must certainly occur. So do not seek to hasten its occurrence, for there is no good for you in it, and no escape for you from it. ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ He is exalted and far above having any partner who could ward off what He wills for them.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *bi-al-ta'* (with the *ta'*, i.e., *fa-la tasta'jiluhu*, in the second person), in keeping with His saying ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾. The rest read *bi-al-ya'* (with the *ya'*, i.e., in the third person), by way of *talwin al-khitab* (shifting of address), or because the address is to the believers, or to them and others besides them. This is due to what is narrated: when ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) leapt up and the people raised their heads, so ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 2:

﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit﴾: with the revelation (*wahy*) or the Qur'an, for it gives life through it to hearts that are dead through ignorance. Or it stands in religion in the place of the spirit in the body. He mentioned it right after that as a sign of the way by which the Messenger ﷺ came to know that their promise would be fulfilled and was near, and to dispel their astonishment that he alone had knowledge of it. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yunazzilu﴾ from *anzala*. Ya'qub read the same, and from him there is also *tanzilu*, meaning *tatanazzalu*. Abu Bakr read *tunzalu*, the imperfect passive from *tanzil*.

﴿by His command﴾: by His command, or for His sake.

﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾: that he take him as a messenger.

﴿that warn﴾: *an* *andhiru*, meaning "that you warn," i.e., "know," from *nadhartu bikadha* when I knew it.

﴿that there is no god but Me, so fear Me﴾: that the matter is that there is no god but Me, so fear Me. Or: warn the people of disbelief and sin that there is no god but Me. His saying ﴿so fear Me﴾ returns to addressing them directly with what is the aim.

The word *an* here is either explanatory (*mufassirah*), since "the Spirit" means revelation that indicates speech. Or it is verbal (*masdariyyah*), in a position of genitive by apposition to "the Spirit," or accusative by removing the preposition. Or it is a lightened form (*mukhaffafah*) of the heavy *anna*.

The verse indicates that the descent of revelation is through the angels, and that its essence is an alert to the oneness of God (*tawhid*), which is the furthest point of the perfection of the theoretical faculty, and a command to piety, which is the highest perfection of the practical faculty. It also indicates that prophethood is a bestowal. The verses after it are evidence of His oneness, insofar as they show that He, exalted is He, is the originator of the roots and branches of the world in accordance with wisdom and benefit. If He had a partner, that partner would be able to do the same, and so mutual hindrance would follow.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 3–4:

﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth.﴾ He brought them into being with a measure, a shape, arrangements and various attributes, which He determined (p-220) and specified by His wisdom. ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ That is, above [having any partner] from among them, or above whatever needs them for its existence or its continuance, or above whatever is unable to create them. In this there is evidence that He, may He be exalted, is not of the kind of physical bodies (ajram).

﴿He created man from a drop (nutfah)﴾, an inanimate thing with no sensation or motion, a fluid that does not hold a fixed form or shape. ﴿Then behold, he is an open adversary﴾, a fluent speaker who argues, ﴿clear⁠﻿﻿﻿—⁠﻿﻿ in proof﴾, or an adversary who openly confronts his Creator, saying: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ It is related that Ubayy ibn Khalaf came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone and said: "O Muhammad, do you think that God will give life to this after it has crumbled?" Then it was revealed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 5–6:

﴿And the cattle﴾: the camels, the cows and the sheep. Its accusative case is governed by an implied verb that this clause explains. ﴿He created them for you﴾. Alternatively, it is in the conjunctive form, coordinated with "the human being" (al-insan) in the preceding verse. "He created them for you" states the purpose for which they were created, and what follows it elaborates on that. ﴿In them is warmth﴾: that by which one is warmed, which protects from the cold. ﴿And benefits﴾: their offspring, their milk and their backs (used for riding and carrying loads). He expressed them as "benefits" so that the term would include what is obtained in exchange for them. ﴿And from them you eat﴾: that is, you eat what is eaten from them, namely the meat, the fat and the milk. The placement of the adverbial phrase "from them" before the verb serves to preserve the rhyme endings (ra'us al-ayy, the closing sounds of the verses). Alternatively, it is because eating from them is the customary and principal means of sustenance. As for eating the other edible animals, it is for the sake of medicine or for enjoyment.

﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾: adornment. ﴿When you bring them home﴾: you return them from their pasture to their enclosure in the evening. ﴿And when you drive them out﴾: you bring them out to the pastures in the morning. The courtyards are adorned by them at both times, and their owners are made honored in the eyes of those who look at them. The bringing home is mentioned first because the beauty in them is most apparent then, for they come back with full bellies and udders swollen with milk, and then they return to the pens, present to their people. The reading "ḥīnan" (حِينًا) is also reported, with "turīḥūna" (تُرِيحُونَ) and "tasraḥūna" (تَسْرَحُونَ) as descriptive clauses for it, with the meaning of "turīḥūna fīhi" and "tasraḥūna fīhi" (at a time in which you bring them home and at a time in which you drive them out).

And it carries your loads (أَثْقَالَكُمْ, i.e., your burdens) — ahmalakum (your loads).

"To a land you could not have reached" — meaning: were it not for the cattle, and had they not been created, you would not have been able, let alone carry them on your backs, to reach it.

"Except with great hardship to yourselves" — that is, except with difficulty and toil. It is also read with a fatha (بِالفَتْحِ, shiqq al-anfus), and that is a dialectal form of it. It has been said that the fatha-vowelled form is a verbal noun from shaqqa al-amr 'alayhi (the matter was hard for him), and its root meaning is "splitting," whereas the kasra-vowelled form (shiqq) means "half," as if half of his strength had gone through fatigue.

"Indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful" — in that He has been merciful to you by creating them for your benefit and by making the matter easy for you.

﴿And the horses and the mules and the donkeys﴾ is conjoined to the cattle (*al-an'am*). ﴿That you may ride them and as an adornment﴾, meaning: that you may ride them and adorn yourselves with them as an adornment.

It has been said that it is conjoined to the position (*mahall*, the grammatical place) of ﴿that you may ride them﴾. The change of construction is because adornment is by the act of the Creator, whereas riding is not by His act. Also, the purpose of creating them is riding, while adorning oneself with them is incidental. It has been read without the conjunction *wa*. On this reading, it may be a reason (*'illah*) for ﴿that you may ride them﴾, or a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial state (*hal*) from one of the two pronouns, meaning: adorning yourselves, or being adorned with them.

It has been cited as evidence for the prohibition of eating their flesh, but there is no proof in it, since attributing an act to a purpose that is generally intended from it does not require that it be intended for nothing else at all. What indicates this is that the verse is Meccan, and the majority of the exegetes and the scholars of hadith hold that domestic donkeys were prohibited in the year of Khaybar. ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾: when He had detailed the animals that people generally need, either necessarily or otherwise, He summarized the rest. It may also be a report that He has among creatures what we have no knowledge of. It may also mean what He created in Paradise and Hell, of which no human heart has conceived.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 9:

﴿And upon Allah rests the showing of the straight way﴾. This means the clarification of the straight path that leads to the truth. Or it means the establishing and rectifying of the way, out of mercy and grace. Or the meaning is: upon Him is the straight way, which whoever travels it will reach without doubt. It is said "sabil qasd" (a straight path) and "qasid," meaning straight, as if it aims at the very direction that the traveller aims for and does not deviate from it. What is meant by ﴿al-sabil﴾ (the way) is the genus, and for this reason He attached the word ﴿qasd﴾ (straightness) to it, and said: ﴿and of it is that which deviates﴾, meaning, swerving away from the straight course or from Allah. The change of style is because it is not incumbent upon Allah Most High to explain the paths of error, or because the intended purpose is the explanation of His way, and the division of the way into the straight and the deviating came only incidentally. It was also read as "minkum jair" (among you is one who deviates), meaning, deviating from the straight course. ﴿And if He had willed﴾, Allah, ﴿He would have guided you all﴾, meaning: if He had willed to guide you all, He would have guided you to the straight way with a guidance that necessarily entails being rightly guided.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 10:

﴿He it is Who sends down water from the sky﴾: from the clouds, or from the direction of the sky. ﴿Some of it is drink for you﴾: that which you drink. ﴿For you﴾ is either a complement of ﴿sends down﴾, or the predicate of ﴿drink﴾ (sharab). ﴿Some of it﴾ (min) is partitive (tab'idiyyah) and is connected to it. Placing it first (taqdim) gives the impression that what is drunk is restricted to it, and there is no harm in this, because the waters of springs and wells are also from it, according to His saying: ﴿then He caused it to flow as springs﴾ and His saying: ﴿then We caused it to settle in the earth﴾. ﴿And from it is trees﴾: from it come trees, meaning the trees on which livestock graze. It has also been said that every plant that grows on the earth is a tree (shajar), as the poet said:

"It feeds them meat when trees (shajar) are scarce... and horses, in feeding them meat, are harmed."

﴿In it you pasture﴾: you graze them, from sامت al-mashiyah and asamaha its owner (i.e., the livestock were sent out to pasture and their owner sent them out). Its root is al-sawmah, which is the mark, because it leaves marks through grazing.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 11:

﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops﴾. Abu Bakr recited it with the nun (نُنْبِتُ, "We cause to grow"), as a form of magnification (al-tafkhim). ﴿And the olives, the date-palms, the grapes, and of all the fruits﴾, and some of all of them, since not every kind of fruit that is possible grows in the land. Perhaps the mention first of what is pastured in (ma yusamu fihi, i.e., pasture-grazed plants) before what is eaten from it (ma yu'kalu minhu) is because it will become animal nourishment, which is the most noble of foods. From this is the placing first of the crops, and the explicit naming of the three kinds and their ordering.

﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who give thought﴾, as evidence of the existence of the Creator (al-Sani') and His wisdom. For whoever reflects that the seed falls into the earth and moisture reaches it and seeps into it, so its upper part splits and the stem of the tree comes out of it, and its lower part splits and its roots come out of it. Then it grows, and from it come out the leaves, the flowers, the spathes, and the fruits, and each of these contains bodies differing in shapes and natures, despite the unity of the materials, and the relation of the lower natures and the celestial influences to the whole, he knows that this is only by the act of a choosing agent, sanctified above contention with opposites and equals. Perhaps the verse was closed with this (i.e., with "who give thought") for this reason.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 12–13:

﴿And He subjected for you the night and the day, and the sun and the moon, and the stars﴾, by readying them for your benefits. ﴿Subjected, by His command﴾: it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to all of them. That is, He benefits you through them while they are subjected to Allah, the Exalted, who created them and governs them as He wills, or [subjected] to that for which they were created, by His bringing them into existence and His decree, or to His judgment. In this there is an announcement of the answer to what might be said, namely that the cause of the growth of plants is the movements of the stars (p-222) and their positions. If that is granted, there is no doubt that they too are contingent in their essence and attributes, and occur in one of the possible ways. Therefore they necessarily need a specifying, choosing, necessarily existent originator, in order to avert circularity (dawr) and infinite regress (tasalsul). Or [the word *musakhkharāt*] is a mimi verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī), pluralized because of the differences in kinds. Ḥafṣ read ﴿and the stars are subjected﴾ as a nominal sentence (mubtada’ and khabar), so that the ruling is generalized after being specified. Ibn ʿĀmir also put the sun and the moon in the nominative. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾: he used the plural of *āyah*, and mentioned intellect (ʿaql) because they indicate several kinds of indication that are evident to those with sound intellects, without needing the exercise of thought, like the states of plants.

﴿And what He has produced for you in the earth﴾ is conjoined to ﴿the night﴾, meaning: and He subjected for you what He created for you in it of animals and plants.

﴿Its colors differ﴾: its kinds, for they differ in color generally. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who remember﴾: their differing in natures, forms and appearances is nothing but by the craftsmanship of a wise Creator.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 16, verse 14:**

﴿And it is He who subjected the sea﴾. He made it such that you are able to benefit from it by riding on it, hunting in it, and diving into it. ﴿That you may eat from it fresh flesh﴾, which is fish. He described it as fresh (*tari*) because it is the most moist of meats, and corruption quickly reaches it, so it is hastened to be eaten. It also shows His power in His creation, that something fresh and sweet (*adhb*) should come forth from salt water (*zu'aq*). Malik (Malik ibn Anas) and al-Thawri (Sufyan al-Thawri) relied on this verse to hold that whoever swears not to eat meat has broken his oath by eating fish. This was answered: the basis of oaths is custom (*'urf*), and by unrestricted usage the word "meat" is not understood to include fish. Do you not see that Allah the Exalted called the disbeliever a beast (*dabbah*), yet the one who swears not to ride a beast does not break his oath by riding him? ﴿And that you may extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾, such as pearls and coral, meaning that your women wear them. It is attributed to you (the men) because they are part of you, and because they adorn themselves with them for your sake. ﴿And you see the ships﴾, meaning the boats, ﴿plowing through it﴾, meaning cutting through it as they run, with their prows (*jawari*) splitting it, from *al-makhr*, which is the cleaving of water. It was said that *mawakhir* means the sound of the ships' motion.

﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾, meaning from the abundance of His provision, by sailing on them for trade. ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾, meaning that you may recognize Allah the Exalted's blessings and thus fulfill their due. The reason gratitude is mentioned after this is that it is the strongest case of bestowal, since He made the places of peril (*mahalik*) a means of benefit and of acquiring livelihood.

And He cast into the earth firm mountains (jibalan rawasiya) lest it should shake with you, (karahata an tamila bikum wa tadtariba), and that is because the earth, before the mountains were created upon it, was a light, simple sphere by nature, and it was fitting for it to move in rotation like the celestial spheres, or to move at the slightest cause of motion. So when the mountains were created upon its surface, its sides became uneven, and the mountains, by their weight, inclined toward the center, so they became like pegs that hold it from moving. It is also said that when God created the earth, it began to sway, so the angels said: "It is not a place of settlement for anyone upon its back," and then it became steady, having been anchored by the mountains. ﴿And rivers﴾: and He made in it rivers, because "cast" (alqa) carries the meaning of "placed" (ja'ala) in it. ﴿And roads, that you may be guided﴾: to your destinations, or to the knowledge of God, glorified and exalted be He.

"and landmarks; and by the star they are guided."

"And landmarks" (ʿalamat): markers by which travellers (al-sabilah) find their way, [such as] mountain, plain, wind, and the like.

"And by the star they are guided" (wa-bil-najmi hum yahtadun): by night, in the deserts and seas. What is meant by "the star" (al-najm) is the genus, and this is indicated by the reading "wa-bil-najmi" with two dammas and a damma with sukun, which is in the plural (ʿala al-jamʿ). It has been said that it refers to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the two Guards (al-Farqadan), the Great Bear (Banat Naʿsh), and the Pole Star (al-Jadi).

Perhaps the pronoun refers to Quraysh, because they were great travellers for trade, well known for being guided by the stars on their journeys. Turning the speech away from its ordinary pattern of address, placing "the star" first, and inserting the pronoun ("hum") is for specification, as if it were said: "And by the star, especially these people, especially they are guided." Therefore reflection on this and gratitude for it are more binding upon them and more obligatory for them.

Verse 17: "Is He then who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?"

[Translation of the commentary:]

﴿Is He then who creates like one who creates not?﴾ This is a denial that comes after the presentation of abundant proofs of His perfect power and the consummate perfection of His wisdom, and of His sole creation of the things He has enumerated among His originations. The one who cannot create anything of those things, but rather cannot bring into existence even a single thing, does not deserve to be equated with Him or to be given a share in His divinity. The natural form of the sentence would have been, "Is one who creates not like one who creates?" but it was reversed as an alert that by associating others with God, Glorified and Exalted is He, they have made Him of the same kind as the impotent created beings, likening Him to them. What is meant by "one who creates not" is everything that is worshipped besides God, Glorified and Exalted is He, with those possessing knowledge among them given precedence in the expression, or the idols; and they are treated as though they were rational beings, because they named them gods, and it is the right of a god to have knowledge. Alternatively, [the mode of expression is used] for the sake of harmony between it and "the one who creates," or for emphasis, as if it were said: "The one who creates is not like the one who creates not among those possessing knowledge, so how much less is that which has no knowledge?" ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ so that you may recognize the corruption of that, for its clarity is such that it is, as it were, already present to the intellect which, with the slightest recollection and attention, comes to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 18–19:

﴿And if you were to count the favours of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ — you would not be able to fix their number, let alone be able to stand up to giving thanks for them. He follows this with an enumeration of the blessings and the establishing of proof of His sole entitlement to worship, as an alert that beyond what He has enumerated there are blessings that cannot be confined, and that the true due of His worship, exalted is He, is beyond one's capacity. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Most Forgiving﴾ — in that He overlooks the shortfall in performing the thanks due for them. ﴿Most Merciful﴾ — He does not cut them off because of your negligence in this regard, nor does He hasten to punish you for your ingratitude toward them.

﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal﴾ — of your beliefs and your deeds. This is a warning and a refutation of polytheism in terms of knowledge, after its refutation in terms of power.

﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you reveal﴾ — of your beliefs and your deeds. This is a warning and a refutation of polytheism in terms of knowledge, after its refutation in terms of power.

(And those whom you invoke besides Allah) — that is, and the deities that you worship besides Him. Abu Bakr read "yad'una" with the ya' (third person). Hafs read all three of them with the ya'. ﴿They create nothing﴾ — when He negated partnership, He clarified who creates and who does not create, and clarified that they create nothing, so that it follows that they do not share in His creation. Then He confirmed that by attributing to them qualities that are incompatible with divinity, so He said: ﴿and they are created﴾, because they are contingent beings whose existence depends on being brought into existence, whereas the god ought to be a necessary existent.

﴿They are dead﴾ — they are dead, never characterized by life; or they are dead presently or in their eventual end. ﴿Lifeless﴾ — not living in their essence, so that it covers every object of worship; whereas the god ought to be living in his essence, not subject to death. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ — and they do not know the time of their resurrection, or the resurrection of their worshippers; so how could there be for them a time of recompense for their worship? **Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 24–25:**

﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ The one who says this is some of them, in mockery, or the delegations that came to them, or the Muslims. ﴿They say, "Legends of the former peoples."﴾ That is, what you claim has been sent down. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 26:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 27:

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾, that is, He will humiliate them or punish them with the Fire, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 35:

﴿And those who associated partners with God said: "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything apart from Him."﴾ They only said this as mockery, or to deny the prophetic mission (ba'tha) and the religious obligation (taklif), holding fast to the principle that what God wills is necessary and what He does not will is impossible, so what is the benefit of them? What follows contains an indication of the answer to the two doubts. ﴿Thus did those who came before them act﴾, so they associated partners with God, forbade what He had made lawful, and rejected His messengers. ﴿So upon the messengers is nothing but the clear conveyance﴾, meaning only the conveying that makes the truth evident. Then he explained that the sending of messengers is a matter that the divine practice (sunna) has followed among all nations, as a cause of guidance for whoever He wills to guide and an increase in misguidance for whoever He wills to misguide, like wholesome food, which benefits and strengthens a sound temperament, and harms and destroys a deviant one, by His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 47:

﴿Or He seizes them through a gradual wasting﴾: that is, while they are in fear, by destroying a people before them so that they become fearful, and then the punishment comes upon them while they are in that fear. Or it means that He reduces them little by little in their persons and their conditions until they perish. The word *takhawwuf* comes from *takhawwaftuhu* when I reduced him (*tanaqqastuhu*).

It is related that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said from the pulpit (*minbar*): "What do you say about this?" They remained silent. Then a shaykh from Hudhayl stood up and said: "This is our dialect: *al-takhawwuf* is *al-tanaqqus* (reduction)." ʿUmar said: "Does the Arabs know that in their poetry?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Our poet Abu Kabir describes his she-camel:"

*Her saddle wore away at her humped, bare-patched back, as the wood of the nabʿa (a tree) wears away the ships.*

Then ʿUmar said: "Keep to your *dīwān* (a collection, here of poetry), and do not go astray." They said: "And what is our *dīwān*?" He said: "The poetry of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era), for in it is the explanation of your Book and the meanings of your speech."

﴿Indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾, in that He does not hasten to punish you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 48:

﴿Have they not looked at what God has created of things?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial (istifham inkar), meaning: they have indeed seen the likes of these crafts, so what is wrong with them that they do not reflect on them, so that the perfection of His power and dominion would become clear to them and they would fear Him. Ma (what) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah) that is vague (mubhamah), and its clarification follows. ﴿Its shadows incline﴾: that is, have they not looked at the created things that have shadows which turn from side to side? Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tarau" (they see) with a ta' (the second person form), and Abu 'Amr read "tatafayya'u" (it inclines) with a ta'.

﴿from the right and the left﴾: from their right sides and from their left sides, that is, from both sides of each one of them. It is a metaphor (isti'arah) taken from the right and left of a person. Perhaps the singular "al-yamin" and the plural "al-shama'il" are used in consideration of the wording and the meaning, just as the singular pronoun in "zilalihi" (its shadows) and the plural in His saying: ﴿prostrating to God, while they are humbled﴾ (sujjadan lillah wa hum dakhirun). These two (sujjadan and dakhirun) are circumstantial clauses (hal) relating to the pronoun in "zilalihi." The meaning of prostration here is submission, whether it is by nature or by choice. It is said: the palm tree "sajadat" when it bends because of the weight of its fruit, and the camel "sajada" when it lowers its head so that it may be ridden. Or "sujjadan" is a circumstantial clause of the shadows, and "wa hum dakhirun" is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun. The meaning is that the shadows return as the sun rises and sets, or through the differences of its risings and settings, by the decree of God the Exalted, from one side to the other, submissive to what has been decreed for them of inclination. Or they fall upon the earth, clinging to it in the form of one prostrating. The bodies themselves are also humbled (dakhirah), that is, abased and subject to the acts of God the Exalted (p-229) within them. The plural of "dakhirun" with the waw-ending is used because among them are those who have reason, or because humbling (duhur) is one of the attributes of rational beings.

It has also been said that "al-yamin wa al-shama'il" refers to the right side of the celestial sphere (falak), which is its eastern side, because the stars appear from it rising and shining, and its left side is the western side opposite to it on the earth. For the shadows at the beginning of the day begin from the east, falling upon the western quarter of the earth, and at midday (zawal) they begin from the west, falling upon the eastern quarter of the earth.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 49–50:

﴿To Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: that is, it submits with a submission that encompasses both submission to His will and His influence, by nature, and submission to His obligation and command, by choice, so that its attribution to the general population of the heavens and the earth is valid. ﴿Of creature﴾ (*min dabbah*) is an explanation of the two, because *dabib* (crawling or moving) is bodily motion, whether it occurs on earth or in the heavens. ﴿And the angels﴾ is coordinated with what was explained by it. Or Gabriel is coordinated with the angels for exaltation, or the immaterial beings are coordinated with the material ones. Those who argued that the angels are immaterial spirits took evidence from this. Or it is an explanation of what is on the earth. Or "the angels" is a repetition of what is in the heavens, specifying it for majesty and magnification. Or the intended meaning is their angels, among them the guardians (*al-hafazah*) and others. Since *ma* (what) is used for rational beings as it is used for others, its use where both categories are gathered is preferable to *man* (who), by giving precedence to rational beings (*taghlib*). ﴿And they do not wax proud﴾ against His worship.

﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾: they fear that He may send a punishment upon them from above, or they fear Him while He is above them in domination, like His saying: "And He is the Subduer over His servants." The clause is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "do not wax proud," or an explanation and confirmation of it, because whoever fears Allah does not wax proud against worshipping Him. ﴿And they do what they are commanded﴾ of obedience and carrying out of affairs. In this is evidence that the angels are under obligation, balanced between fear and hope.

﴿And Allah said: "Do not take two gods; He is only one God. So fear Me alone."﴾ He mentioned the number, although the thing counted (the "two") is already indicated by it, to show that the purpose of the prohibition is directed at it, or as a hint that duality (*al-ithnaniyya*) contradicts divinity (*al-uluhiyya*, the state of being God). Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 53–55:

﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. That is: whatever blessing has come to you, it is from Allah. ﴿Whatever﴾ (ma) is either conditional, or a relative pronoun that implicitly carries the sense of a condition, with regard to the report and not to the occurrence. For the settling of the blessing upon you is a cause for the report that it is from Allah, not for its coming to you from Him. ﴿Then when harm touches you, to Him you cry for help﴾: so you do not humble yourselves except to Him. Al-ju'ar (crying out) is raising the voice in supplication and seeking aid.

(p-230) ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you﴾, namely your unbelievers, ﴿associate others with their Lord﴾ by worshipping other than Him. This is if the address is general. If it is specific to the polytheists, then min (of) is for explanation, as if he said: "behold, a group, namely you". It is also permissible for min to be partitive, with the sense that only some of them are considered, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when He brought them safely to land, some of them are moderate﴾.

﴿So that they may deny what We have given them﴾ of the blessing of the removal of harm from them, as if they intended by their polytheism the ingratitude for the blessing, or the denial that it is from Allah, exalted is He. ﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾ is a command of threat. ﴿For you will soon know﴾ intensifies its warning. It was also read as (fa-yumatta'u), passive, in coordination with ﴿so that they may deny﴾; and on this reading it is permissible for the lam to be the lam of command used for threat, and the fa for the consequent.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 56–57:

﴿And they assign to what they do not know﴾ That is, to their gods which have no knowledge, because they are inanimate objects, so that the pronoun in ﴿what﴾ refers to them; or to those which they do not know, so that they hold about them ignorant beliefs, such as that they will benefit them and intercede for them, in which case the returning pronoun to "what" is omitted; or on account of their ignorance, in which case "what" is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya) and the object of the assignment (al-majʿūl lahu) is omitted because it is known. ﴿a portion of what We have provided them﴾ from the crops and livestock. ﴿By God, you will certainly be questioned about what you used to fabricate﴾ regarding the claim that they are gods truly deserving of being drawn near to; and this is a warning to them concerning it.

﴿And they assign to God daughters﴾ Khuzaʿa and Kinana used to say, "The angels are the daughters of God." ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ is a declaration of His transcendence above their statement, or an expression of wonder at it. ﴿And for themselves is what they desire﴾ meaning sons. It is permissible in "what they desire" to read it in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and in the accusative by coordination with "daughters," on the basis that the verb "assign" (al-ja'l) carries the meaning of "choose" (al-ikhtiyar). Although this leads to the subject and object pronoun referring to one and the same thing, it is not far-fetched to permit this in the coordinated element.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 58–59:

﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female⁠—﴾ he is informed of her birth. ﴿His face becomes dark⁠﴾ becomes, or remains, so for the whole day. ﴿Black⁠﴾ from grief and from shame before the people. The blackening of the face is a metaphor (kinayah) for distress and disgrace. ﴿And he is filled with suppressed rage (kazim)⁠﴾ full of fury at the woman.

﴿He hides himself from the people⁠﴾ he conceals himself from them. ﴿Because of the evil of what he has been given good news of⁠﴾: from the evil of the thing announced, by custom. ﴿Shall he keep it⁠﴾ speaking to himself, reflecting on whether to leave it alive. ﴿In humiliation⁠﴾ in disgrace ﴿or bury it in the dust⁠﴾ that is, conceal it in it and bury it alive. The pronoun is masculine in agreement with the word ﴿ma⁠﴾ (what), and it is also read with feminine agreement in both places.

﴿Evil is what they judge!⁠﴾ since they assign to the One exalted above having offspring what they themselves regard as something to be rejected.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 58–59:

﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female⁠—﴾ he is informed of her birth. ﴿His face becomes dark⁠﴾ becomes, or remains, so for the whole day. ﴿Black⁠﴾ from grief and from shame before the people. The blackening of the face is a metaphor (kinayah) for distress and disgrace. ﴿And he is filled with suppressed rage (kazim)⁠﴾ full of fury at the woman.

﴿He hides himself from the people⁠﴾ he conceals himself from them. ﴿Because of the evil of what he has been given good news of⁠﴾: from the evil of the thing announced, by custom. ﴿Shall he keep it⁠﴾ speaking to himself, reflecting on whether to leave it alive. ﴿In humiliation⁠﴾ in disgrace ﴿or bury it in the dust⁠﴾ that is, conceal it in it and bury it alive. The pronoun is masculine in agreement with the word ﴿ma⁠﴾ (what), and it is also read with feminine agreement in both places.

﴿Evil is what they judge!⁠﴾ since they assign to the One exalted above having offspring what they themselves regard as something to be rejected.

For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the attribute of evil (مَثَلُ السَّوْءِ, mathal al-saw'). It is the attribute of need for offspring, which calls for death, the preservation of males to bolster themselves with them, and the aversion to females and burying them alive out of fear of poverty.

﴿And to Allah belongs the highest attribute﴾ (al-mathal al-a'la), which is necessary existence in Himself, absolute self-sufficiency, surpassing generosity, and freedom from the attributes of created beings.

﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾, the One who alone possesses perfect power and wisdom.

(p-231) ﴿And if God were to seize mankind for their wrongdoing﴾ — for their disbelief and their disobediences. ﴿He would not leave upon it﴾ — upon the earth — ﴿any creature.﴾ He has left out the explicit mention, since it is understood from the reference to mankind and to the creature. ﴿Any creature﴾ — at all — on account of the ill-omen of their wrongdoing.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him: "The dung beetle nearly perished in its burrow because of the sin of the son of Adam, or of a wrongdoing creature."

It has been said: "If the fathers were destroyed for their disbelief, the sons would not exist."

﴿But He defers them until a specified term﴾ — which He appointed for their lifespans, or for their punishment, so that they may beget offspring. ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ Rather, they perish or are punished at that time without fail. The generality of "mankind," and the attribution of wrongdoing to them, does not require that they all be wrongdoers, including the prophets, peace be upon them, since it is permissible that what is widespread among them and issued from most of them be attributed to them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 62:

﴿And they attribute to Allah that which they dislike﴾ i.e., that which they dislike for themselves: daughters, partners in leadership, contempt for the messengers, and base wealth. ﴿And their tongues describe the lie﴾ along with that, namely ﴿that for them is the best (al-husna)﴾, i.e., with Allah, as in His saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I shall have with Him the best (al-husna)﴾. It was also read as "al-kudhub," the plural of kadhub (liar), as an attribute of "al-alsina" (the tongues). ﴿Undoubtedly (la jaram) for them is the Fire﴾: a rejection of their statement and an affirmation of its opposite. ﴿And that they will be mufratun﴾: brought forward (muqdimun) to the Fire, from afrattuhu (I sent him ahead) in seeking water, when I send it ahead.

Nafi' read it with a kasra on the ra' (mufrirun), on the basis that it derives from al-ifrat (excess) in sins. It was also read with shadda: with a fatha (mufarratun), from farratuhu in seeking water, and with a kasra (mufarritun), from al-tafrit (negligence) in acts of obedience.

By Allah, We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you, but Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them, so they persisted in their ugly deeds and disbelieved in the messengers. ﴿So he is their guardian today﴾, i.e., in this world. He expressed "today" as a reference to its time; or [it means] "so he is their guardian at the time when he was adorning [their deeds] for them"; or [it refers to] the Day of Resurrection, with the statement being a narration of a past or future state. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the Quraysh, i.e., Satan made their deeds attractive to the earlier disbelievers, and he is the guardian of these [Quraysh] today, inciting them and leading them astray. If a noun is understood to be omitted, [the meaning would be]: "so he is the guardian of their likes," and the guardian (walī) means the companion (qarīn) or the helper (nāṣir), in which case it is a negation of any helper for them in the most emphatic manner. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them﴾ for the people ﴿that over which they differ﴾: concerning the Oneness of God (tawhid), divine decree (qadar), the states of the afterlife (ma'ad), and the rulings on human actions. ﴿and as a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe﴾. These two are conjoined (ma'tufan) to the grammatical position (maḥall) of ﴿li-tubayyina﴾ (in order that he may make clear), because they are both the effects of the sent-down Book, unlike the act of making clear.

﴿And God sends down water from the sky, and with it gives life to the earth after its death﴾: He caused various kinds of vegetation to grow in it after it had dried up. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾: listening with reflection (tadabbur) and fairness (insaf).

And indeed in the cattle there is a lesson for you (﴿وَإنَّ لَكم في الأنْعامِ لَعِبْرَةً﴾): a sign through which one passes from ignorance to knowledge. ﴿We give you to drink of what is in their bellies﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining the lesson. He mentioned the pronoun and made it singular here in consideration of the wording (lafz), but made it feminine in Surat al-Mu'minun in consideration of the meaning (ma'na), since ﴿al-an'am﴾ (the cattle) is a collective noun (ism jam'). For this reason Sibawayh counted it among the nouns of plural pattern built on the forms of af'al, such as akhlaq and akyas. As for one who says it is the plural of ni'am, he makes the pronoun refer to a part, since the milk belongs to some of them and not to all of them; or to its singular; or it refers to it according to meaning, since what is intended by it is the genus. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read (nasqikum) with a fathah here and in al-Mu'minun.

﴿from between dung and blood, milk﴾: it creates it from some parts of the blood, which is produced from the fine parts that are in the dung, and the dung is the food that has been digested to some extent in the rumen (kirsh). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that when the beast grazes and the fodder is cooked in its rumen, its lowest part becomes dung, its middle part milk, and its upper part blood. If this report is authentic, what is meant is that its middle part becomes the material of milk and its upper part the material of the blood that nourishes the body, because neither of these forms in the rumen. Rather, the liver draws the pure essence of the food digested in the rumen and leaves its residue, which is the dung. Then it holds the essence for a while until it digests it a second time, producing four humours along with a watery substance. The discerning faculty (al-quwwa al-mumayyiza) then separates that watery substance, distinguishing what exceeds the needed amount from the two, and sends it to the kidneys, the gall bladder and the spleen. Then the remainder is distributed among the organs according to their need, flowing to each its due in the manner suited to it, by the decree of the All-Wise, the All-Knowing. Then, if the animal is female, its humours exceed the amount of its nourishment because cold and moisture dominate its temperament, so the excess is first pushed to the womb for the sake of the foetus. When the foetus is separated, that excess, or part of it, pours into the udders, where it is whitened by the proximity of their glandular flesh, and so it becomes milk. Whoever contemplates Allah's craftsmanship in producing the humours and milks, preparing their places and channels, the causes that generate them and the powers that transform them at every time in the manner suited to them, will be compelled to acknowledge the perfection of His wisdom and the boundlessness of His mercy.

The first ﴿min﴾ is partitive (tab'idiyya), since the milk is a part of what is in their bellies. The second is a source-indicating ﴿min﴾ (ibtida'iyya), as in your saying: "I drank from the pool," since between the dung and the blood is the place from which the giving of drink begins. It is related either to ﴿nusqikum﴾, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿laban﴾ (milk), placed before it because it is indefinite, and to draw attention to the fact that this is the locus of the lesson.

﴿pure﴾: clear, not carrying the colour of blood or the smell of dung; or purified from the thick parts that accompany it, by the narrowing of its passage. ﴿Palatable to the drinkers﴾: easy to pass down their throats. It has also been read as "sayyigh" with shaddah and without it.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 67:**

﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes﴾ is dependent on an elided verb (muta'alliq bi-mahdhuf), meaning: "and We give you to drink from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes," that is, from their juice (ʿaṣīr). His words ﴿you take from it an intoxicant (sakaran)﴾ are either a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) explaining the giving of drink, or they are connected to ﴿you take﴾. The pronoun "from it" (minhu) repeats the adverbial phrase for emphasis (ta'kid), or it is the predicate (khabar) of an elided subject whose description is ﴿you take﴾, meaning: "and from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes is a fruit from which you take." The pronoun is masculine in the first two readings because it refers to the elided genitive-noun (muḍāf maḥdhūf), which is "the juice," or because "fruits" (thamarāt) is understood as "fruit" (thamar). "Sakar" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) which has been used as a name for wine (khamr).

﴿And good provision (rizqan ḥasanan)﴾ refers to dates, raisins, date syrup (dibs), and vinegar (khall). If the verse came before the prohibition of wine, it indicates its disapproval; otherwise it combines reproach with a reminder of favour (minnah).

It has been said that "sakar" means nabidh (a fermented drink), and it has been said that it means food, as in the line of poetry:

*"I made the honour of the noblemen an intoxicant"*

meaning: I lived off their honour. It has also been said that "sakar" is whatever satisfies hunger, so that "provision" refers to what is obtained from its prices.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who use reason (ya'qilun)﴾: they employ their intellects through contemplation and reflection upon the signs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 68–69:

﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾: He inspired it (alhamahā) and cast it into their hearts. It is also read "ilā al-naḥali" with two fatḥahs. ﴿That take for yourselves﴾: with an-ittakhidhī (the an being the verbal particle). It is permissible that an be explanatory (mufassira), because in the inspiration (al-īḥā') there is the meaning of speech (al-qawl), and the feminine pronoun is according to the sense, since the naḥl (bee) is masculine. ﴿Houses in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they erect﴾: it is mentioned with the particle of partitiveness (ḥarf al-tab'īḍ) because it does not build in every mountain, every ((p-233)) tree, and everything that is trellised with a vine or a roof, nor in every place of them. What it builds is called a house (bayt) so that it may make honey in it, by analogy with human building, because of the excellence of its craftsmanship and the soundness of its division, which the most skilled engineers cannot achieve except with instruments and precise observation. Perhaps its mention is to draw attention to this. It is also read (bīūtan) with a kasrah on the bā'. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read (ya'rushūna) with a ḍammah on the rā'.

﴿Then eat from all the fruits﴾: from every fruit that you desire, bitter and sweet. ﴿Then travel﴾: what you have eaten. ﴿The ways of your Lord﴾: in His paths, in which He transforms, by His power, the bitter juice into honey from your bellies. Or ﴿travel﴾ the ways which He inspired you to use in making honey; or travel returning to your houses ﴿the ways of your Lord﴾ that are not rugged for you and not confusing. ﴿Docile (dhululan)﴾: the plural of dhalūl, and it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the ways, meaning made easy, which Allah the Exalted made smooth and easy for you; or it is from the pronoun in "fa-usluki", meaning while you are docile, submissive to what you have been commanded. ﴿There comes forth from their bellies﴾: as if He turned away from addressing the bee to addressing the people, because they are the object of the favour, and the purpose of creating the bee and inspiring it is for their sake. ﴿A drink﴾: meaning honey, because it is something drunk. Whoever claims that the bee eats flowers and fragrant leaves, which transform in its belly into honey, and then vomits it for storage for winter, has used this as evidence; and whoever claims that it gathers with its mouths tender, sweet, small particles scattered over leaves and flowers and places them in its houses for storage, so that when much of it has gathered in its houses it becomes honey, has interpreted "bellies" as "mouths." ﴿Its colours vary﴾: white, yellow, red and black, according to the differences in the age of the bees and the season. ﴿Wherein is healing for mankind﴾: either by itself, as in phlegmatic diseases, or with other things, as in the rest of diseases, since rarely is there any electuary (ma'jūn) in which honey is not a component. Moreover, the indefiniteness (al-tankīr) in it indicates partitiveness, and it is permissible that it be for magnification (lil-ta'ẓīm).

It is related from Qatadah that a man came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "My brother complains of his stomach." He said: "Give him honey to drink." He went away, then returned and said: "I have given him to drink, but it did not benefit him." He said: "Go and give him honey to drink, for Allah has spoken the truth and the belly of your brother has lied." So he gave him to drink, and Allah the Exalted healed him, and he was cured, as if he had been released from a fetter.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, or to what Allah has explained of the states of the bee. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾: for whoever contemplates the bee's distinction in those subtle sciences and wondrous acts with true contemplation, knows with certainty that there must be a capable, wise Creator who inspires it with that and drives it toward it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 70:

﴿Allah created you, then He causes you to die﴾ at differing terms. ﴿And among you is one who is brought back﴾, that is, returned, ﴿to the most abject age﴾, the most degraded of life, meaning senility (al-haram), which resembles childhood in the diminishing of strength and of intellect. It was said that it is ninety-five years, and it was said seventy-five.

﴿So that he knows nothing after having known﴾, so that he comes to a state resembling the state of childhood in forgetfulness and poor understanding. ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of the measures of your lifespans, ﴿All-Powerful﴾, who causes the vigorous youth to die and leaves the decrepit, perishing old man alive. In this there is an admonition that the variation in people's terms is nothing but by the decree of a Powerful, Wise One, who fashioned their frames and balanced their temperaments according to a known measure. Had that been required by natures, the variation would not have reached this extent.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 71:

﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision.﴾ So among you are the wealthy and among you are the poor, and among you are the masters (mawali) who dispense their own provision and the provision of others, and among you are the slaves (mamalik) whose condition is otherwise. ﴿Those who have been favoured will not hand over their provision﴾ to ﴿what their right hands possess﴾, i.e., to their slaves (mamalik). For what they give to them is their provision which Allah has placed in their hands. ﴿So they are equal in it﴾: the masters and the slaves are equal in that Allah has provided for them. The clause is either necessarily related to the preceding negated clause or confirms it. It may also be that it stands in the place of an answer, as if it had been said: "Why do those who have been favoured not hand over their provision to what their right hands possess, so that they would be equal in provision?" On this reading, it is a rebuke and a denunciation of the polytheists, for they associate with Allah some of His creatures in divinity, yet they are not content for their slaves to share with them in what Allah has bestowed upon them, so that they would be equal to them in it. ﴿Then do they deny the favour of Allah?﴾ by taking partners for Him. For it requires that some of what Allah has bestowed be attributed to them, and that they deny it is from Allah; or [it means] because they rejected such arguments after Allah had bestowed their clarification upon them. The preposition (ba' in bi-ni'mati) is used because denial (judud) implies disbelief (kufr). Abu Bakr read "tajhadun" (with ta') in view of His words ﴿khalaqakum﴾ and ﴿faddala ba'dakum﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 72:

﴿And Allah has made for you, from your own selves, spouses﴾, i.e., of your own kind, so that you may find tranquility in them, and so that your offspring may be like you. It is said that it refers to the creation of Hawwa' (Eve) from Adam.

﴿And has made for you, from your spouses, sons and grandchildren (ḥafadah)﴾, and descendants of descendants, or daughters. For the ḥāfid (grandchild, or servant) is one who hastens in service, and daughters serve in the houses in the most complete manner. It is said that they are the sons-in-law (akhtān) through the daughters. It is said that they are the stepchildren (rabā'ib). It is permissible that by them is meant the sons themselves, and the conjunction (waw) is for the difference between the two descriptions.

﴿And has provided for you from the good things﴾, from the delicious things or the lawful things. The word ﴿min﴾ (from) is for partitive meaning, for what is provided in this world is a sample of them.

﴿Then in falsehood do they believe?﴾, namely that the idols benefit them; or that among the good things are some that are forbidden, such as the baḥā'ir and the sawā'ib.

﴿And in the favor of Allah do they disbelieve?﴾, in that they attributed His blessings to the idols, or that they forbade what Allah had made lawful for them. The placing of the prepositional phrase (ṣilah) before the verb is either for emphasis, or to give the impression of restriction for the sake of hyperbole, or to preserve the rhyme (fawāṣil).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 73:

﴿And they worship besides Allah that which owns for them no provision from the heavens and the earth, [any] at all﴾ — [provision] of rain and plants. And ﴿provision﴾, if you make it a verbal noun (masdar), then ﴿at all﴾ (shay'an) is in the accusative governed by it; otherwise it is a substitute (badal) for it. ﴿And they are not able﴾ — to take possession of it, or they have no ability whatsoever. The pronoun is plural in it but singular in ﴿owns﴾ because ﴿ma﴾ is singular in meaning, referring to the gods. It is also permissible for it to refer to the disbelievers, meaning: and these [people] are not able, although they are living beings who act freely, to [possess] any of that at all, so how [much less] inanimate matter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 74–75:

﴿So do not strike out similitudes for Allah﴾ That is: do not make for Him any likeness to which you associate Him, or by which you measure Him. For striking a similitude is the comparison of one state with another. ﴿Indeed, Allah knows﴾ the corruption of what you rely on of analogy, [namely] that the worship of a king's slaves is included in the honouring of his worship, and that your sin in what you do is grave. ﴿while you do not know﴾ that; had you known it, you would not have dared to do it. This is a reason (ta'līl) for the prohibition. Or it means that He knows the essence (kunh) of things while you do not know it, so abandon your opinion in preference to His text. It is also possible that what is meant is: "So do not strike out similitudes for Allah, for He knows how similitudes are to be struck, while you do not know." Then He taught them how a similitude is struck, so He struck a similitude for Himself and for those who are worshipped besides Him, and said:

﴿Allah strikes a similitude: a slave owned, who has no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, so that he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal?﴾ He made the likeness of what is associated with Him the owned slave, utterly incapable of any disposal, and made Himself the likeness of the free owner whom Allah has provided with much wealth, so that he disposes of it and spends from it as he wishes. He argued, by the impossibility of partnership and equality between the two, despite their sharing in the category of being created, for the impossibility of equating the idols, which are the most incapable of creatures, with Allah, the self-sufficient, who is absolutely capable.

(p-235) It has also been said that this is an illustration of the forsaken disbeliever and the successful believer. The restriction of the slave by ownership serves to distinguish him from the free man, for he too is a slave of Allah. The removal of power serves to distinguish him from the mukātab (the slave contracted to buy his freedom) and the ma'dhūn (the slave licensed to trade). Placing him as a counterpart to the owner who disposes [of his property] indicates that the owned slave does not own anything. The more apparent view is that the word "man" (man) is an indefinite qualified noun, so as to agree with "a slave." The plural pronoun in ﴿they are equal﴾ is because it refers to both categories, for the meaning is: "Are free men and slaves equal?" ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ All praise belongs to Him entirely; no one else deserves it, let alone worship, because He is the source of all blessings. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ so they attribute a blessing to other than Him and worship that other on account of it.

Then He taught them how a similitude is struck, so He struck a similitude for Himself and for those who are worshipped besides Him, and said:

﴿Allah strikes a similitude: a slave owned, who has no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, so that he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal?﴾ He made the likeness of what is associated with Him the owned slave, utterly incapable of any disposal, and made Himself the likeness of the free owner whom Allah has provided with much wealth, so that he disposes of it and spends from it as he wishes. He argued, by the impossibility of partnership and equality between the two, despite their sharing in the category of being created, for the impossibility of equating the idols, which are the most incapable of creatures, with Allah, the self-sufficient, who is absolutely capable.

(p-235) It has also been said that this is an illustration of the forsaken disbeliever and the successful believer. The restriction of the slave by ownership serves to distinguish him from the free man, for he too is a slave of Allah. The removal of power serves to distinguish him from the mukātab (the slave contracted to buy his freedom) and the ma'dhūn (the slave licensed to trade). Placing him as a counterpart to the owner who disposes [of his property] indicates that the owned slave does not own anything. The more apparent view is that the word "man" (man) is an indefinite qualified noun, so as to agree with "a slave." The plural pronoun in ﴿they are equal﴾ is because it refers to both categories, for the meaning is: "Are free men and slaves equal?" ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ All praise belongs to Him entirely; no one else deserves it, let alone worship, because He is the source of all blessings. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ so they attribute a blessing to other than Him and worship that other on account of it.

And God strikes a parable: ﴿two men, one of them dumb﴾, born mute and deaf, who neither understands nor can make himself understood. ﴿He has no power over anything﴾ of the crafts and affairs, because of the deficiency of his intellect. ﴿And he is a burden upon his master﴾: a dependant and a weight upon whoever is in charge of his affairs. ﴿Wherever he directs him﴾: wherever his master sends him on some matter. It is recited as *yuwajjahu* (in the passive voice, "is directed") and as *yuwajjih* (with the meaning of *yatawajjah*, "turns"), like the line of poetry: "Wherever I turn, throw me upon Sa'd." It is also recited as *tawajjaha* in the past tense (*qira'ah*, a recognised variant reading). ﴿He brings no good﴾: no success and no adequacy in an important matter. ﴿Are they equal, he and one who commands justice﴾, who is an understanding, articulate, capable and rightly guided person, benefiting people by urging them to justice, which comprises all the virtues? ﴿And he is on a straight path﴾: he himself is on a straight path, and does not set out toward any goal without reaching it with the nearest effort. The reason these attributes are matched with these two descriptions is that they are the perfection of what is opposite to them. This is a second parable which God struck for Himself and for the idols, to nullify any partnership between Him and them, or it is for the believer and the disbeliever.

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾: His knowledge is specific to Him, and no one other than Him knows it. It is what is hidden in them from the servants, in that it is not perceptible and no perceptible thing points to it. It is said that it refers to the Day of Resurrection, since its knowledge is hidden from the people of the heavens and the earth. ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a blink of the eye﴾: the matter of the establishment of the Hour, in its swiftness and ease. ﴿Or it is nearer﴾: its matter is nearer than that, in that it occurs in the time of half that movement, or rather in the very instant in which the movement begins, for He, exalted is He, brings the creatures to life all at once, and what comes into being all at once occurs in an instant. ﴿Or﴾ is for choice (takhyir), or it carries the meaning of ﴿bal﴾ (rather). It is said that its meaning is that the establishment of the Hour, even if it is delayed, is with Allah like the thing you say is ﴿as a blink of the eye﴾ or ﴿nearer﴾, as an intensification in regarding it as near. ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾: so He is able to bring the creatures to life all at once, just as He was able to bring them to life gradually. Then He pointed to His power, saying: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the bellies of your mothers﴾. Al-Kisa'i read the hamza with a kasra (ﺇ), on the basis that it is a dialect form or an assimilation to what precedes it. Hamzah read it with a kasra and a kasra on the mim, and the hā' is an added letter, like its counterpart in ﺃﻫﺮﺍﻕ (ahrāqa). ﴿You knew nothing﴾: ignorant, retaining the ignorance of inanimacy. ﴿And He made for you hearing and sight and hearts﴾: as instruments by which you learn, so that through your senses you perceive particular things and apprehend them, then through your hearts you become aware of the points of agreement and difference among them, through repeated sensation, until the self-evident knowledge (al-'ulum al-badihiyyah) is attained for you, and you become able to acquire the acquired indicators (al-ma'alim al-kasbiyyah) by reflecting upon them. ﴿That you may be grateful﴾: so that you may know what He has bestowed upon you, stage after stage, and thus give thanks for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 79:

(p-236) ﴿Have they not seen the birds, made subservient in the midst of the sky?﴾ Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah and Yaʿqub read it with the ta' (﴿ترَوْا﴾ in the second person), taking it as addressed to the general public. ﴿Subservient﴾ means made subject and easy for flight, by means of the wings and the suitable means with which they were created for it. ﴿In the midst of the sky﴾ means in the air, which is distant from the earth.

﴿None holds them up there﴾ in it, ﴿except Allah﴾, for the weight of their bodies requires that they fall, and there is no suspension above them nor support beneath them to hold them up.

﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ of the subjection of birds to flight, in that He created them with a constitution which makes flight possible for them, and created the air such that flight in it is possible and their being held up in the air is contrary to their natural disposition. ﴿For a people who believe﴾, because it is they who benefit from them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 80:

﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling place﴾ — a place in which you dwell at the time of your residence, like the houses made of stone and clay; "sakan" is a verb in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul).

﴿And He has made for you, from the hides of livestock, tents﴾ — these are the domed tents made of leather (adam). It is permissible that it includes tents made of wool, fleece and hair, since they, insofar as they grow upon their hides, truly are said to be "from their hides."

﴿You find them light﴾ — you find them light, so that carrying and moving them is easy for you.

﴿On the day of your departure﴾ — at the time of your travelling (tirhal).

﴿And on the day of your residence﴾ — and setting them up or pitching them at the time of settling in or stopping.

The two Hijazi and the two Basran readers recited ﴿yawma dh'anikum﴾ with a fatha, and it is a dialectal form of it.

﴿And from their wool, their fur, and their hair﴾ — wool is for sheep, fur (wabar) is for camels, and hair (sha'r) is for goats. Its attribution to the pronoun of ﴿al-an'am﴾ is because these are part of its totality.

﴿Furniture (athath)﴾ — what is worn and spread out.

﴿And provision (mata')﴾ — what is traded with.

﴿For a time (ila hin)﴾ — for a period of time, since, because of their firmness, they remain for a lengthy duration; or until the time of your death; or until you have fulfilled your needs from them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 81:

﴿And Allah has made for you, out of what He has created,﴾ [of the trees, the mountains and the buildings, and other things] ﴿shade,﴾ by which you protect yourselves from the heat of the sun.

﴿And He has made for you, among the mountains, shelters﴾ [places in which you dwell, from the caves and the houses hewn out of them]; the plural of kinn (shelter). ﴿And He has made for you garments﴾ [clothes made of wool, flax, cotton and other materials] ﴿which protect you from the heat﴾. He mentioned it specifically, either by being content with one of the two opposites, or because protection from heat was more important to them. ﴿And garments which protect you from your violence﴾ meaning coats of mail and quilted armour; the word sirbal (garment) covers everything that is worn. ﴿Thus﴾ [like the completion of these blessings that have been mentioned before] ﴿He completes His blessing upon you, that you may submit﴾ meaning that you may reflect upon His blessings, so that you believe in Him and yield to His judgement. It has also been read as ﴿taslamun﴾ (you may be safe), from salama (safety), meaning that you give thanks and thereby are safe from punishment, or that you reflect upon them and thereby are safe from polytheism. It has also been said that ﴿taslamun﴾ means you are safe from wounds by wearing armour.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 82–83:

﴿Then if they turn away﴾ — they turned away and did not accept from you. ﴿Then your duty is only to convey the clear message﴾ — so it should not harm you; your duty is only to convey, and you have conveyed. This is the placing of the cause in the position of the effect (iqamat al-sabab maqam al-musabbab).

﴿They recognize the favour of Allah﴾ — that is, the polytheists recognize the favour of Allah which He enumerated for them and others, in that they acknowledge it and acknowledge that it is from Allah, exalted is He. ﴿Then they deny it﴾ — by worshipping other than the One who bestowed it, and their saying that it is by the intercession of our gods, or due to such-and-such a cause, or by their neglect of its due rights. It has also been said that the favour of Allah is the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ): they recognized it through the miracles, then they denied it out of obstinacy. The meaning of "then" (thumma) is the remoteness of denial after recognition. ﴿And most of them are the disbelievers﴾ — the ones who deny out of obstinacy. He mentioned "most" either because some of them did not know the truth (p-237) due to deficiency of intellect or negligence in reflection, or because the proof was not established against them since they had not reached the age of obligation; or because "most" is used in place of the whole, as in His saying: ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 84:

﴿And on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness﴾, and he is their prophet, who bears witness for them and against them concerning belief and disbelief. ﴿Then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved﴾ to offer excuses, since they have no excuse. It was also said that it refers to returning to the world. And ﴿then﴾ (thumma) is for the increase in what befalls them of the severity of being prevented from making excuses, because of the total despair it brings regarding what they had been hoping for, namely the testimony of the prophets, peace be upon them. ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾, meaning they will not be asked to seek to please [God], from al-'utba (ʿutba), which is al-ridha (contentment, pleasure). The accusative of "yawma" (the Day) is governed by an implied verb, whose estimate is "remember" (udhkur), or "warn them" (khawwif-hum), or "what befalls them befalls them." Likewise His saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 85–86:

﴿When those who did wrong see the punishment﴾: the punishment of Hell. ﴿It will not be lightened for them﴾: i.e., the punishment. ﴿Nor will they be given respite﴾: they will not be granted a reprieve.

﴿When those who associated partners [with God] see their partners﴾: their idols which they claimed to be partners, or the devils who shared with them in disbelief by inciting them to it. ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to invoke besides You"﴾: whom we used to worship or obey. This is an acknowledgment that they were in error in that, or a plea that their punishment be halved. ﴿But they will throw back at them the word: "Indeed you are liars"﴾: i.e., they will answer them with denial, [denying] that they were God's partners, or that they did not actually worship them but rather worshipped their own desires, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿No! They will deny their worship of them﴾. It is not impossible that God would make the idols speak on that occasion. Or [the denial concerns] that they had led them into disbelief and compelled them to it, as in His words: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you and you responded to me﴾.
