Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 89:

﴿And [remember] the Day when We raise up in every community a witness against them from among themselves﴾. That is, their prophet, for the prophet of every community was sent from among them. ﴿And We bring you, O Muhammad, as a witness against these﴾, that is, against your community. ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾: this is a fresh statement (isti'naf), or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) with qad understood (bi-idmar qad).

﴿As an exposition﴾ (tibyanan), a clear exposition, ﴿of all things﴾ of the matters of religion, either in detail or in summary, by referral to the Sunnah (al-Sunnah, the prophetic practice) or to analogy (qiyas, analogical reasoning).

﴿And as guidance and mercy﴾ for all, and the deprivation of the one deprived is only due to his own neglect. ﴿And as glad tidings for the Muslims﴾ in particular.(p-238)

﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice﴾, meaning moderation in matters. In belief, it is like *tawhid* (affirming God's oneness), which lies between *ta'til* (denying God's attributes) and *tashrik* (associating partners with God). And in the doctrine of *kasb* (acquisition of actions), it lies between pure *jabr* (compulsion) and *qadar* (free will). In practice, it is like devotion through performing obligatory duties, which lies between idleness (*bitala*) and asceticism (*tarahhub*). In character, it is like generosity, which lies between stinginess and extravagance. ﴿And beneficence﴾, meaning excellence in acts of obedience. This is either in quantity, such as voluntary supererogatory acts (*nawafil*), or in quality, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Excellence is that you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, [know that] He sees you." ﴿And giving to kinsfolk﴾, meaning giving relatives what they need. This is a specification after a generalization, for emphasis. ﴿And He forbids indecency﴾, meaning excess in pursuing the appetitive faculty, such as fornication, for it is the most vile and shameful state of a human being. ﴿And wrongdoing﴾, meaning what is disapproved of in the one who engages in it, through stirring the irascible faculty. ﴿And oppression﴾, meaning seeking superiority and dominance over people and tyrannizing them. This is the satanic trait that results from the imaginative faculty (*al-quwwa al-wahmiyya*). No evil comes from a human being except that it falls under these categories, arising through one of these three faculties. Therefore Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It is the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for both good and evil." It became the cause of the conversion to Islam of Uthman ibn Maz'un (may Allah be pleased with him). Had the Qur'an contained nothing but this verse, it would have been true of it that it is "an explanation of everything, and guidance and mercy for the worlds." Perhaps its placement right after His words ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾ is to draw attention to this. ﴿He admonishes you﴾, through commands, prohibitions, and distinguishing between good and evil. ﴿So that you may remember﴾, meaning that you may take heed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 91:

﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾ meaning the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) upon Islam, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah﴾. It has been said: it means every matter that must be fulfilled, and His saying ﴿when you make a covenant﴾ does not suit this. It has also been said: it means vows (nudhur). And it has been said: it means faith in Allah. ﴿And do not break the oaths﴾, i.e., the oaths of the pledge of allegiance, or oaths in general. ﴿After their confirmation﴾, after they have been strengthened by mentioning the name of Allah, Exalted is He. From this (root) comes the word akkada, in which the waw is changed to a hamzah. ﴿And you have indeed made Allah your surety﴾, a witness to that pledge, for the surety (kafil) watches over the condition of the one for whom he stands surety and is a guardian over him. ﴿Indeed, Allah knows what you do﴾, of breaking the oaths and covenants.

﴿And do not be like her who unravels her yarn﴾ *mā ghazalathu* (what she spun): a *maṣdar* (verbal noun) used in the sense of the passive participle (*maf'ūl*), meaning "what she spun." ﴿After its strengthening﴾: this phrase is connected to ﴿unravels﴾, meaning she unravels her yarn after it has been twisted and firmly made. ﴿Into shreds﴾ *ankāthan*: strands whose twist has been undone; it is the plural of *nakath*. Its position is as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative) from ﴿her yarn﴾, or as the second object of ﴿unravels﴾, since the verb carries the sense of "makes it." The purpose is to liken the one who breaks the oath to someone of this condition.

It is said that she was Rayṭa bint Saʿd ibn Taym al-Qurashiyya, for she was foolish and used to do this. ﴿Taking your oaths as means of deceit among you﴾ is a *ḥāl* from the pronoun in ﴿do not be﴾, or from the prepositional phrase that takes the place of the predicate. That is: do not be those who resemble a woman of this condition, making your oaths a source of corruption and deceit among you. The root meaning of *dakhal* is that which enters a thing and is not part of it. ﴿That one community may be more numerous than another﴾: that one group may be greater in number and more abundant in wealth than another group. The meaning is: do not break faith with a people because of your numerical superiority or inferiority, or because of the greater or lesser strength of those who oppose you, like Quraysh. For when they saw a force among the enemies of their allies, they broke their covenant and allied themselves with their enemies. ﴿Surely Allah tests you thereby﴾: the pronoun refers to ﴿that one community may be more numerous﴾, because it carries the sense of a verbal noun. That is, He tests you by their being more numerous, so that He may see whether you hold fast to the cord of fidelity to the covenant of Allah and the pledge to His Messenger, or whether you are deceived by the multitude of Quraysh and their strength and by the fewness and weakness of the believers. It is also said that (p-239) the pronoun refers to *al-rabāʾ* (excess gain), and it is said that it refers to the command to fulfil the covenant. ﴿And He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ﴾: when He recompenses you for your deeds with reward and punishment.

﴿If God had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, agreed upon Islam. ﴿But He leads astray whom He wills﴾ by forsaking (*khidhlan*, abandonment by divine withdrawal of help), ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾ by granting success (*tawfiq*). ﴿And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do﴾, a questioning of rebuke (*tabkit*) and recompense.

﴿And do not make your oaths a means of deception among yourselves﴾. This is an explicit prohibition after an implicit one (*tadmin*, implication), for emphasis and to stress how ugly the forbidden act is.

﴿Lest a foot slip﴾, that is, from the path of Islam (*mahajjat al-Islam*). ﴿after it had been firmly planted﴾ upon it. The intended meaning is their feet. He used the singular and indefinite form to show that the slipping of a single foot is grave, so how much more so the slipping of many feet. ﴿And you would taste evil﴾, meaning punishment in this world. ﴿for what you hindered from the way of God﴾, either by your hindering yourselves from fulfilling (the oath) or by hindering others from it, for whoever breaks the pledge (*bay'ah*) and apostatizes sets that as a precedent for others. ﴿And for you there will be a great punishment﴾ in the Hereafter.

﴿If God had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, agreed upon Islam. ﴿But He leads astray whom He wills﴾ by forsaking (*khidhlan*, abandonment by divine withdrawal of help), ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾ by granting success (*tawfiq*). ﴿And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do﴾, a questioning of rebuke (*tabkit*) and recompense.

﴿And do not make your oaths a means of deception among yourselves﴾. This is an explicit prohibition after an implicit one (*tadmin*, implication), for emphasis and to stress how ugly the forbidden act is.

﴿Lest a foot slip﴾, that is, from the path of Islam (*mahajjat al-Islam*). ﴿after it had been firmly planted﴾ upon it. The intended meaning is their feet. He used the singular and indefinite form to show that the slipping of a single foot is grave, so how much more so the slipping of many feet. ﴿And you would taste evil﴾, meaning punishment in this world. ﴿for what you hindered from the way of God﴾, either by your hindering yourselves from fulfilling (the oath) or by hindering others from it, for whoever breaks the pledge (*bay'ah*) and apostatizes sets that as a precedent for others. ﴿And for you there will be a great punishment﴾ in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 95:

﴿And do not sell the covenant of Allah for a little price﴾ — i.e., do not exchange the covenant of Allah and the pledge of allegiance to His Messenger (ﷺ) ﴿for a little price﴾, a fleeting goods (ʿaraḍ) of little value, namely what the Quraysh used to offer to the weak among the Muslims, and stipulate for them, on condition that they apostatise (irtidad). ﴿Indeed, what is with Allah﴾ of victory and booty in this world, and reward in the Hereafter ﴿is better for you﴾ than what they promise you. ﴿If you only knew﴾ — i.e., if you are among the people of knowledge and discernment (tamyiz).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 96:

﴿What is with you﴾ of the transient goods of this world. ﴿will run out﴾, i.e., will come to an end and perish. ﴿And what is with Allah﴾ of the treasuries of His mercy ﴿is lasting﴾, i.e., does not run out. This is a justification for the preceding ruling and evidence that the bliss of the people of Paradise is lasting. ﴿And We will surely reward those who patiently persevered their reward﴾ for enduring poverty and the harm of the disbelievers, or for enduring the hardships of the obligations. Ibn Kathir and Asim read it with the nun (﴿lanajziyanna﴾, "We will surely reward"). ﴿According to the best of what they used to do﴾, i.e., according to the best of their deeds, those whose performance is weightier, such as the obligatory and the recommended acts, or with a reward better than their deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 97:

﴿Whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female﴾ He specified both sexes to remove any restriction (to one of them). ﴿And is a believer﴾, since no account is taken of the deeds of disbelievers in deserving reward; what is hoped for them is only a lightening of the punishment. ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ in this world: he lives a good life. If he is well-off, this is evident; and if he is poor, his life is made good through contentment, acceptance of what has been apportioned to him, and the expectation of a great reward in the Hereafter. By contrast, the disbeliever: if he is poor, the matter is evident; and if he is well-off, greed and fear of losing what he has do not leave him free to enjoy his life. It has also been said that the good life is in the Hereafter. ﴿And We will surely reward them with their best deeds﴾ of obedience.

(p-240) ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾ meaning, when you intend to recite it, like His saying, ﴿When you rise to prayer﴾. ﴿Seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾, that is, ask God to protect you from his whisperings, lest he whisper to you during the recitation. The majority hold that this is for recommendation (istihbab). And there is in it evidence that the one praying seeks refuge in every rak'ah, because the ruling that is consequent upon a condition recurs with the recurrence of that condition, by analogy. And its being followed by mention of righteous action and the promise for it is an indication that seeking refuge at the time of recitation is of this kind.

And on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud: "I recited before the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and I said: 'I seek refuge in the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan.' He said: 'Say: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. Thus did Gabriel recite it to me from the Pen, from the Preserved Tablet.'" ﴿Indeed, he has no authority﴾, that is, no dominion or sway, ﴿over those who believe and upon their Lord they rely﴾, that is, over the friends of God, the believers in Him and those who rely upon Him. For they do not obey his commands, nor do they accept his whisperings, except in what they consider trivial, through momentary lapse and heedlessness. For this reason they were commanded to seek refuge. So He mentioned the lack of authority after the command to seek refuge, lest it be supposed from it that he has authority.

﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾, that is, love him and obey him, ﴿and those who, through him, are associating partners﴾, that is, with God, or because of Satan.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 101:

﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse﴾ by way of abrogation (naskh), so that We make the abrogating verse (al-ayah al-nasikhah) take the place of the abrogated one (al-mansukhah), either in wording or in ruling. ﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ of the benefits (maslahat). Perhaps what is a benefit at one time becomes a corruption after it, so He abrogates it; and what is not a benefit at that time is a benefit now, so He establishes it in its place. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (yunazzilu) with the lightened form (al-takhfif). ﴿They say﴾, i.e., the disbelievers. ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ (muftari), one who invents lies against Allah, commanding something and then a change of mind appears to you, so you forbid it. This is the response (jawab) of "idhan" (then). ﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiradh) to rebuke the disbelievers for their statement and to draw attention to the corruption of their basis. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ the wisdom of the rulings, and they do not distinguish the error from the correct.

Al-Baydawi, *Anwar al-Tanzil*, commentary on Surah 16, verse 102:

﴿Say: "The Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) has sent it down from your Lord in truth"﴾. He means Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. The attribution of "Spirit" to "Holiness" (al-Quds), which means purity, is like their saying "Hatim al-Jud" (Hatim of generosity). Ibn Kathir read "Ruh al-Qudus" with lightening (takhfif), meaning the second word is read with a sukun, not a shaddah. The verbs ﴿yunazzilu﴾ and ﴿nazzalahu﴾ (both forms of "to send down") are a reminder that its descent was gradual, according to what the interests required, in a way that necessitated substitution (al-tabdil). ﴿from your Lord in truth﴾ means accompanied by wisdom. ﴿to make firm those who believe﴾ means that God makes firm those who believe in faith, in the belief that it is His speech, and that when they hear the abrogating (al-nasikh) revelation and reflect on what it contains of the consideration of benefit and wisdom, their beliefs become firmly established and their hearts are at rest. ﴿and as a guidance and good tidings for the Muslims﴾, who submit to His judgment. These two words are conjoined to the locus (mahall) of the phrase ﴿li-yuthabbita﴾, meaning: as firmness, guidance and good tidings. There is in this an allusion to the occurrence of the opposites of these things for others. ﴿li-yuthabbita﴾ was also read with lightening (takhfif).

We know well that they say, "It is only a human being who teaches him." They mean Jabr, the Roman slave of Amir ibn al-Hadrami. It was also said that they were Jabr and Yasar, who used to make swords in Makkah and would recite the Torah and the Gospel, and the Messenger (ﷺ) would pass by them and listen to what they recited.

(p-241) It was also said that it was 'A'ish, the slave of Huwaytib ibn Abd al-'Uzza, who had embraced Islam and was a man of books. It was also said that it was Salman al-Farisi. ﴿The tongue of the one to whom they point is foreign.﴾ This is the language of the man toward whom they incline their speech away from uprightness. The word is derived from *lahd al-qabr* (the niche dug in the side of a grave). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *yalhadūna* (يَلْحَدُونَ) with a fatha on the *ya* and the *ha*, meaning "they deviate" (*ilhad*, distortion of the truth). *Lisanun a'jamiyyun* (لِسانٌ أعْجَمِيٌّ) means a foreign tongue that is not clear. ﴿And this﴾ means this Qur'an. ﴿Is a clear Arabic tongue﴾ meaning one possessing clarity and eloquence. The two sentences are resumptive, in order to refute their slander. Its explanation admits two aspects.

The first: what he heard from him is foreign speech which neither he nor you understand, whereas the Qur'an is Arabic, which you understand with little reflection. How, then, could what he took from him be the Qur'an?

The second: suppose he learned the meaning by listening to his speech, yet he did not take the wording from him, because that is foreign and this is Arabic. And the Qur'an, just as it is miraculous in respect of its meaning, is miraculous in respect of its wording too. Moreover, the many sciences contained in the Qur'an cannot be learned except through lasting companionship with a teacher who excels in those sciences over a long period. So how could he have learned all of that from a lowly boy (*ghulam suqi*) who heard from him, during some passing moments, foreign words whose meanings perhaps they did not even know? Their slander of the Qur'an with such weak words is proof of the extremity of their impotence.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 104–105:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾ do not accept that they are from Allah. ﴿Allah will not guide them﴾ to the truth, or to the path of salvation. It is also said: to Paradise. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter. He threatened them for their disbelief in the Qur'an after he had removed their doubt and repelled their slander against it, then he turned the matter back upon them and said:

﴿Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies﴾ because they do not fear a punishment that would restrain them from it. ﴿And those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those who disbelieved, or to the Quraysh. ﴿They are the liars﴾ i.e., the liars in reality, or the most complete in lying, because denying the signs of Allah and slandering them with these fables is the greatest lie; or those whose habit is lying, whom neither religion nor manly honour restrains from it; or the liars in their saying: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ and ﴿Only a human is teaching him﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 16, verse 106:

﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief﴾ is a *badal* (substitution, a grammatical replacement) for "those who do not believe," and what lies between them is a *i'tiraḍ* (parenthetical clause). Or it is a substitution for "those" (*ulā'ika*), or for "the liars." Or it is a *mubtada'* (grammatical subject) whose *khabar* (predicate) is omitted, indicated by His words, ﴿upon them is wrath﴾. It may also be in the accusative by way of censure (*dhamm*). And *man* may be a conditional (*shartiyyah*) whose apodosis (*jawab*) is omitted, indicated by His words, ﴿except one who is compelled﴾ to fabricate or to utter a word of disbelief. The exception is an *istithna' muttasil* (contiguous exception), because disbelief (*kufr*) linguistically encompasses both speech and conviction, just as belief (*iman*) does. ﴿And his heart is at rest with faith﴾: his creed has not changed. In this is evidence that faith is assent of the heart. ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾: he believes in it and is content with it. ﴿Upon them is wrath from God, and theirs is a great punishment﴾, since nothing is greater than their crime.

It is narrated: "Quraysh compelled ʿAmmar and his parents, Yasir and Sumayya, to apostasy. They tied Sumayya between two camels, and a spear was brought to her private parts, and they said: 'You embraced Islam only for the sake of men.' So she was killed, and they killed Yasir. They were the first two slain in Islam. ʿAmmar gave them with his tongue what they wanted, being compelled. It was said: 'O Messenger of God, ʿAmmar has disbelieved.' He said: 'Never! Indeed ʿAmmar is filled with faith from his head to his feet, and faith has mixed with his flesh and blood.' ʿAmmar came to the Messenger of God ﷺ weeping, and the Messenger of God ﷺ began wiping his eyes and saying: 'What is with you? If they return to you, return to them with what you said.'"

This is evidence for the permissibility of uttering disbelief under compulsion, although it is more excellent to abstain from it, in order to honor the religion, as his parents did. It is also narrated: "Musaylima seized two men. He said to one of them: 'What do you say about Muhammad?' He said: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ.' He said: 'What do you say about me?' He said: 'You too.' So he released him. Then he said to the other: 'What do you say about Muhammad?' He said: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ.' He said: 'What do you say about me?' He said: 'I am deaf.' He repeated this to him three times, and each time he gave the same answer, so he killed him. This reached the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: 'As for the first, he took the concession of God. As for the second, he proclaimed the truth, so congratulations to him.'"

﴿That﴾ refers to disbelief after faith, or to the threat. ﴿Because they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter﴾: because they gave it precedence over it. ﴿And that Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾: that is, those who are disbelievers in His knowledge, [He does not guide] to what would make faith firm, and does not protect them from deviation.

﴿They are the ones upon whose hearts and hearing and sight Allah has set a seal﴾: so they refused to perceive the truth and to reflect upon it. ﴿And they are the heedless﴾: those who are complete in heedlessness, since their present condition has made them neglect reflection on the outcomes.

﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers﴾: because they wasted their lives and spent them on what led them to the everlasting punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 110–111:

﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried,﴾ i.e., were tormented, like ʿAmmar (may Allah be pleased with him), ﴿[He is] with forgiveness and mercy.﴾ The word "then" (thumma) indicates the distance between the state of these people and the state of those others. Ibn ʿĀmir read (fatanū) with a fatha, meaning: after they had tormented the believers, like al-Ḥaḍramī, whose master forced his slave, compelling him, until he apostatized, then embraced Islam and emigrated.

﴿Then they strove and were patient﴾ in the struggle and in the hardships that befell them. ﴿Indeed your Lord, after these,﴾ i.e., after the emigration, the struggle and the patience, ﴿is surely All-Forgiving﴾ of what they did before, ﴿Most Merciful﴾, bestowing favour upon them as a reward for what they did afterwards.

﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾: this is in the accusative case governed by ﴿Most Merciful﴾, or by "remember." ﴿Pleading for itself﴾ means arguing on behalf of its own self and striving for its own deliverance, not concerned with the affair of anyone else, so that it says, "Myself, myself." ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it did,﴾ as recompense for what it did. ﴿And they will not be wronged,﴾ meaning their rewards will not be diminished.

﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town﴾, meaning He made it an example for every people upon whom Allah had bestowed blessings, but the blessing made them insolent and they disbelieved, so Allah sent down His vengeance upon them. Or [the parable refers] to Makkah. ﴿It was secure and at peace﴾, so that fear did not disturb its people. ﴿Its provision came to it﴾, meaning its sustenance. ﴿Abundantly﴾, meaning in ample measure.

﴿From every place﴾, meaning from its various regions. ﴿But it denied the favors of Allah﴾, meaning His blessings. The word *ni'am* is the plural of *ni'ma* with the *ta'* omitted, since the plural is not being counted, as in *dir'* and *adra'* (the plural of *dir'*, "coat of mail"). Alternatively, it is the plural of *nu'm*, as *bu's* is the plural of *ba's* in *bu's* and *ab'us*. ﴿So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾. He used the metaphor of *dhawq* (tasting) for perceiving the effect of harm (*isti'ara*, metaphor, the transfer of a word from its literal to a figurative sense). The garment is used for what covered them and enveloped them of hunger and fear. The verb of "making taste" was attributed to it by considering the thing to which the metaphor refers, as in the verse of Kathir:

*Abundant in the cloak when he smiles laughing... the necks of wealth were bound by his laughter.*

Here he used the metaphor of "cloak" for kindness, because it protects the honor of its possessor as a cloak protects what is cast upon it. He attributed to it "abundance" (*ghamr*), which is a description of kindness and bounty and not a description of a cloak, looking to the thing to which the metaphor refers. Sometimes the metaphor itself is considered, as in his saying:

*My cloak is disputed by the servant of 'Amr... slowly, O brother of 'Amr ibn Bakr!*

*Mine is the share that my right hand possesses... and take from it a share, wrapping yourself with it.*

He used "cloak" as a metaphor for his sword, then said "wrap yourself," looking to the metaphor itself. ﴿For what they used to do﴾, meaning for their deeds.

And certainly there came to them a Messenger from among them, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). The pronoun refers to the people of Makkah, returning to mention them after He had mentioned their parable.

"But they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers," that is, the punishment that befell them while they were in the state of being entangled in wrongdoing and punishment was severe drought (al-jadb), or the battle of Badr.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 114–115:

﴿So eat of what God has provided for you, lawful and good﴾. He commanded them to eat what God had made lawful for them and to give thanks for the blessings He had bestowed upon them, after He had restrained them from disbelief and threatened them with what He had mentioned of the parable and the punishment that befell them, as a deterrent for them from the practices of the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyyah) and its corrupt doctrines. ﴿And give thanks for God's blessing, if it is Him you worship﴾: obey Him; or, if your claim that you intend by worshipping the idols to worship Him is true.

﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than God has been invoked. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. When He commanded them to partake of what He had made lawful for them, He enumerated for them its prohibited things, so that it would be known that whatever lies beyond them is lawful for them. Then He reinforced that by forbidding declaring things unlawful or lawful according to their own whims, so He said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 116–117:

﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾, as they said, ﴿"What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males"﴾, and so on. The context of the discourse and the opening of the sentence with *innama* (only) require that the prohibited things be restricted to the four categories, except for what is added to them by evidence, such as predators and domestic donkeys. The word ﴿al-kadhiba﴾ (the lie) is in the accusative, governed by ﴿do not say﴾, and ﴿"This is lawful and this is unlawful"﴾ is either an apposition to it, or it is related to ﴿describe﴾ with the verb "say" implied, meaning: "Do not say the lie about what your tongues describe, so that you say, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful.'" Alternatively, ﴿al-kadhiba﴾ is the object of ﴿describe﴾, and *ma* is a verbal-noun (*masdariyya*) particle, meaning: "Do not say, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful,' for the describing by your tongues of the lie," that is: do not forbid or permit by a mere utterance your tongues pronounce without evidence. He described their tongues as describing the lie as an intensification of describing their speech as false, as though the reality of the lie were unknown and their tongues were describing it and knowing it through this speech of theirs. For this reason it is counted among eloquent expressions, like their saying: "Her face describes beauty, and her eye describes magic." It has been read as ﴿al-kadhibi﴾ in the genitive, in apposition to *ma*. *Al-kadhibu* is the plural of *kadhub* or *kaddhab*; in the nominative it is an attribute of ﴿al-alsina﴾ (the tongues), and in the accusative it is for dispraise, or it means "the false words." ﴿"So that you may fabricate against God the lie"﴾ is a causal clause that does not contain the purpose. ﴿"Indeed, those who fabricate against God the lie will not prosper"﴾. Since the fabricator fabricates to attain a desired end, He negated prosperity from them and clarified it by His saying:

(p-244) ﴿"A brief enjoyment"﴾, that is, what they fabricate for its sake, or what they are in, is a small benefit that will cease soon. ﴿"And for them is a painful punishment"﴾ in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 118:

﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade what We have related to you﴾ That is, in Surat al-An'am, in His words: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾. ﴿Before this﴾ is related either to ﴿related﴾ or to ﴿forbade﴾. ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by the prohibition. ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ in that they did what they were punished for. In this there is an indication of the difference between them and others in the prohibition, and that just as it may be for harm, it may also be for punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 119:

﴿Then, indeed, your Lord – for those who did evil in ignorance﴾ [i.e., on account of it, or while being entangled in it], so that ignorance of Allah and of His punishment, and failure to reflect on the consequences, would be general, due to the dominance of desire. And "evil" (al-su') encompasses both slandering Allah and other things. ﴿Then they repented after that and reformed; indeed, your Lord, after it﴾ [i.e., after repentance], ﴿is Forgiving﴾ [of that evil], ﴿Merciful﴾ [He rewards those who turn back in repentance].

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verses 120–122:

﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation (ummah)﴾ because of his perfection and his gathering of virtues that are hardly ever found except scattered among many persons, as in his saying:

"It is not far-fetched for God / that He should gather the world into one."

He was the leader of the monotheists (muwahhidun) and the model of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun), who disputed with the sects of the polytheists and refuted their deviant doctrines with decisive proofs. For this reason he followed his mention with the exposure of the doctrines of the polytheists: their associationism, their slander against prophethood, and their prohibition of what God had made lawful. Or it is because he alone was a believer while the rest of the people were unbelievers.

It has also been said that ummah here is an form (fi'lah) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like rihlah (a journey) and nukhbah (the elite), from amma-hu (he aimed for him) or iqtada bihi (he followed him), since people would turn to him to benefit from him and follow his way, as in God's saying: ﴿Indeed, I am making you an imam for the people﴾.

﴿Devoutly obedient to God﴾: obedient to Him, standing upright in carrying out His commands.

﴿Upright (hanif)﴾: inclining away from falsehood.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾: as they claimed, for the Quraysh used to claim that they were upon the religion of Abraham.

﴿Grateful for His blessings﴾: he is described with the word "qillah" (few) to alert that he would not neglect thanking for small blessings, so how much more for great ones.

﴿He chose him﴾: for prophethood. ﴿And guided him to a straight path﴾: in calling to God. ﴿And We gave him good in this world﴾: by making him beloved to the people, so that the lords of the religions befriended him and praised him, and by granting him good offspring and a long life in ease and obedience. ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾: among the people of Paradise, as he asked when he said: ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 124:

﴿Indeed, the Sabbath was only made﴾: the glorification of the Sabbath, or setting oneself apart therein for worship. ﴿For those who differed concerning it﴾: that is, concerning their prophet. They were the Jews, whom Musa (peace be upon him) commanded to devote themselves to worship on Friday, but they refused and said: "We want Saturday, because He (exalted is He) finished the creation of the heavens and the earth on it." So God obliged them to observe the Sabbath and made the matter strict upon them. It has also been said that the meaning is: the Sabbath was only made a burden, which is the transformation (into apes and swine), upon those who differed concerning it, for they permitted hunting on it at one time and forbade it at another, and they devised stratagems to get around it. He mentioned them here to threaten the polytheists, just as He mentioned the town that disbelieved in the blessings of God. ﴿And indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾: by requiting them for their differing, or by requiting each group with what it deserves.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 125:

﴿Call﴾ those to whom you have been sent. ﴿To the way of your Lord﴾: to Islam. ﴿With wisdom﴾: with a firm, well-constructed argument, which is the proof that makes the truth clear and removes doubt. ﴿And with good admonition﴾: persuasive addresses and beneficial lessons. The first is for calling the elite of the community who seek realities, and the second is for calling their common folk. ﴿And argue with them﴾: and argue with their obstinate opponents. ﴿In the way that is best﴾: in the best manner of argumentation, which is gentleness, softness, choosing the easier course, and premises that are most widely accepted, for that is more effective in calming their fervor and clarifying their confusion. ﴿Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best who are guided﴾: that is, your duty is only to convey and to call. As for the attainment of guidance and misguidance, and the recompense for them, these are not up to you; rather, God knows best those who are astray and those who are guided, and He is the one who recompenses them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 16, verse 126:

﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished.﴾ When He commanded him to invite (to the faith) and explained to him its methods, He alluded to him and to those who follow him, (commanding them) to abandon opposition and to observe justice with those who are hostile to them, for the invitation (to the faith) cannot be separated from this, insofar as it involves rejecting customs, abandoning desires, disparaging the religion of the forefathers, and passing judgment upon them as disbelievers and misguided.

It is said that when he (ﷺ) saw Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him), who had been mutilated, he said: "By Allah, if Allah grants me victory over them, I will mutilate seventy men in your place," and then (this verse) was revealed. So he expiated for his oath. In it is evidence that the one who takes retribution may match the wrongdoer, but he may not exceed it. And (the verse) urges pardon, by allusion in His words: ﴿And if you punish﴾, and explicitly, in the more emphatic manner, in His words: ﴿But if you are patient, it is indeed better for those who are patient﴾, i.e., patience (is better) than retaliation for those who retaliate. Then He explicitly commanded this to His Messenger, because he was the most worthy of people of it, owing to his greater knowledge of Allah and his greater trust in Him, so He said:

﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah﴾, meaning, except by His enabling (*tawfiq*) and steadfastness (*tathbit*). ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, meaning over the disbelievers, or over the believers and what was done to them. ﴿And do not be in distress at what they plot﴾, meaning in constriction of the chest (*dayq al-sadr*) because of their scheming. Ibn Kathir read ﴿فِي ضَيْقٍ﴾ with a kasra here and in Surat al-Naml. Both forms are dialects, like *al-qawl* and *al-qīl* (فِي ضِيقٍ). It is also possible that *al-ḍayq* is a lightened form of *ḍiyq*.

﴿Indeed Allah is with those who are mindful of God (*taqwa*)﴾, meaning those who guard against sins. ﴿And those who are doers of good﴾, meaning in their deeds, through devotion and grace. Or, ﴿with those who are mindful of Allah﴾ by magnifying His command, ﴿and those who are doers of good﴾ through compassion toward His creation.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Nahl, Allah will not call him to account for what He bestowed upon him in the abode of this world. And if he dies on the day or night in which he recites it, he will have a reward like that of one who died and left the best bequest (*al-wasiyya*)."
